svg.title: Nature & childhood
svg.desc: The Schoolboy: meaning: Blake’s child enjoys nature but suffers under fearful schooling. Bird-in-cage and damaged-plant images link restriction to lost development. Cruel eye: authority becomes surveillance. Appeals to parents make adults responsible for the future. Blake: how it works: Six five-line stanzas; songlike pattern contrasts with confinement. Questions demand an answer rather than accepting adult power. Context: childhood and resistance to restrictive authority. Compare Catrin’s mother–child conflict. Wordsworth: meaning: A solitary walker finds company in dancing daffodils. Later, the inward eye brings the scene back. Personification moves the flowers’ dance into the heart. The gain is emotional wealth. Wordsworth: how it works: Four six-line stanzas, ABABCC. Final stanza shifts from past encounter to recurring present pleasure. Romantic nature, imagination and personal feeling. Solitude becomes rewarding, unlike the opening loneliness. Blackberry Picking: meaning: Heaney’s remembered childhood moves from eager collecting to rotten fruit. Sensory attraction becomes disgust. Blood, eyes and Bluebeard imagery add unease. Desire outlasts knowledge of inevitable decay. Heaney: how it works: Long first stanza gathers excitement; shorter second stanza reverses it. Rural Northern Irish childhood informs concrete details. Compare: Wordsworth preserves pleasure through memory; Heaney cannot preserve fruit. Blake blames restriction, not natural decay.
